question: Which of the following best captures why accrual accounting, despite being more complex than cash accounting, is mandatory for listed companies in India and globally?
before: Accrual accounting is mandatory because it captures economic reality — not just cash movement. By recognising revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, accrual accounting produces a faithful representation of how a business actually performed in a period, even when cash timing distorts the picture. This is what allows analysts to compare TCS's performance to Infosys's, or one quarter to another, in a meaningful way. Cash basis accounting would make a company that just collected on a 5-year-old invoice look more profitable than one that just delivered ₹500 Cr of fresh services — clearly nonsensical for performance evaluation. Option A is cynical and wrong — accrual accounting requires more judgment, but the principles (matching, conservatism, substance over form) are designed to constrain manipulation, not enable it. Option C is wrong — accrual accounting is universal across all major capital markets (US GAAP, IFRS, Ind AS) because economic logic, not regulatory copying, demands it. Option D is wrong — accrual accounting is harder to audit, which is why audit fees are high and audit standards are detailed. The deeper truth: accrual is the price you pay for economic accuracy in a world where business and cash do not move in lockstep.
after:
Concept: Accrual accounting recognises revenues when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of cash timing. This matching principle produces an accurate financial picture by aligning costs with the revenues they generate, enabling valid period-to-period and cross-company comparisons.

Why this is correct: Accrual accounting captures economic reality rather than just cash flows. A business that delivers ₹500 Cr of services but has not yet collected cash should show that revenue in the current period, and the matching expenses should offset it — not wait months or years until cash arrives. This makes financial statements comparable across time and between companies. For instance, comparing TCS and Infosys requires both to measure profit the same way; cash accounting would distort results whenever collection or payment timing shifts, making analysis meaningless.

Why the others are wrong:

Option A: Accrual accounting actually constrains manipulation, not enables it. The matching principle, conservatism, and substance-over-form requirements are designed to ensure judgment is applied consistently and defensibly, not to create loopholes. More judgment is required, but auditors and regulators hold companies accountable for the reasonableness of accrual choices.

Option C: Accrual accounting is not a regulatory copy — it is universal across all major capital markets (US GAAP, IFRS, Ind AS) because the economic logic is the same everywhere. When revenue and cash do not move in lockstep, cash-only accounting fails to represent performance. This fundamental principle, not regulatory imitation, drives the mandate.

Option D: Accrual accounting is harder to audit, not easier. The need for judgment on provisioning, revenue recognition, and expense timing makes audits more complex, which is why audit fees are higher and audit standards are detailed. Option D inverts the reality.

Intuition: Equity analysts rely on accrual earnings to spot true operational performance beneath cash timing noise. A company might have strong cash flow in one quarter simply because a large customer paid an old invoice, while actual revenue generation was weak — accrual accounting reveals the truth. This is why listed companies globally are required to use accrual accounting: it is the only way to make financial statements economically meaningful.
